Lousy
LOU-zee
adjective (Silent Generation slang)
From louse (Old English lūs), plural lice. Lousy meant literally "infested with lice" in Middle English, and was already a term of contempt for a mean or vile person by the late 1300s. The broad slang sense — poor, rotten, inferior, miserable ("a lousy meal," "I feel lousy") — spread in American speech in the early 20th century and was carried everywhere by the soldiers of both World Wars, who knew the literal sense from the trenches and the barracks. By the 1940s and 1950s it was the everyday complaint word of the Silent Generation, and "lousy with" (swarming with: "the town was lousy with cops") rode along beside it.

Biblical Definition

When your grandfather was a boy, lousy was the all-purpose word for anything that disappointed him: a lousy movie, lousy weather, a lousy hand of cards, a lousy day at the plant. The men who came home from the war had earned the word honestly — they had lived with real lice in foxholes and troopships, and everything bad after that was simply lousy. The word is not filthy, and a grandparent who used it was not sinning by the word itself. But it is worth noticing what the word is usually for. It is the word of the complaint. Israel in the wilderness had a lousy word for the manna too: "our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes" (Num 11:6), and Scripture records that "when the people complained, it displeased the LORD" (Num 11:1). God once sent real lice on Egypt as a judgment (Exo 8:17), and the Christian who calls every small trouble "lousy" is in danger of treating ordinary providence as if it were a plague. Paul, who had been beaten, shipwrecked, and jailed, wrote instead, "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content" (Php 4:11), and commanded the church, "Do all things without murmurings and disputings" (Php 2:14). That contentment is not a stiff upper lip; it is the fruit of knowing Christ, who has given us Himself, so that "in every thing" we can "give thanks" (1Th 5:18). A lousy day in the hands of a good Father is never only lousy.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (from Middle English "full of lice"; broadened by two World Wars) for poor, rotten, miserable — the everyday word of complaint, which Scripture answers with contentment and thanks in every thing (Php 4:11).

expand to see more

LOUSY, adj. (Silent Generation slang, 1910s–50s; GI staple of both World Wars) Poor, inferior, rotten; miserable or ill. "What a lousy break." "I feel lousy today." Also lousy with: swarming with, full of.

Webster (1828) — LOUS’Y, adjective s as z. [louse.] 1. Swarming with lice; infested with lice. 2. Mean; low; contemptible; as a lousy knave.

Decode for families: when Grandpa says "lousy," he means bad; the old literal meaning (crawling with lice) is why the word sounded so strong.

Key Scripture

Num 11:1 — "And when the people complained, it displeased the LORD: and the LORD heard it; and his anger was kindled; and the fire of the LORD burnt among them, and consumed them that were in the uttermost parts of the camp."

Exo 8:17 — "And they did so; for Aaron stretched out his hand with his rod, and smote the dust of the earth, and it became lice in man, and in beast; all the dust of the land became lice throughout all the land of Egypt."

Php 4:11 — "Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content."

Php 2:14 — "Do all things without murmurings and disputings:"

1Th 5:18 — "In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you."

Modern Corruption

A plain, unprofane word whose only danger is its use: it is the natural vocabulary of grumbling, and Scripture calls the believer from murmuring to contentment and thanks.

expand to see more

There is nothing wrong with saying a meal was lousy when it was. Honest description is not sin. The trouble is the habit the word feeds. A family can fall into a rhythm in which every day, every teacher, every boss, and every Sunday sermon is lousy, and that rhythm is the murmuring that Israel practised in the wilderness. God heard it as complaint against Himself, because it was: the manna they called worthless was His daily gift (Num 11:1).

The cure is not a ban on the word but a change of heart. Paul learned contentment "in whatsoever state" (Php 4:11) because his state was in Christ’s hands. A grandparent who once called the whole Depression lousy and then thanked God at supper for beans and bread was teaching the right lesson, whatever word he used.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English lūs (louse) → Middle English lousy (full of lice; vile) → early 20th c. American slang (poor, rotten) → WWI–WWII GI usage → Silent Generation everyday complaint word.

Usage
